en: We have become polled cattle.
We have withered like autumn grass
And been left utterly undone.
The royal summer pasture where the people grazed,
Where we migrated in splendor and tethered mares—
We can no longer encamp there.
We have become like a perfectly level plain
Over which the waters spread.
Bereft of our shepherd,
We have become like sheep.
All these dear people gathered here,
While our noble lion lived,
Dwelt in the Ala-Too and drove their herds,
A people peacefully encamped.
By day we laughed, by night we played—
Such a people we once were.
Who did not jauntily wear
The sable hat upon his head?
While we had wealth and fortune,
Who did not stride about proudly?
When they saw our warrior lion,
The watchful enemy quailed.
Üyrü-Maral and Kümüsh-Tak,
Where are the uplands where the people autumned?
He joined what had been severed
And gathered what had been scattered.
He rekindled extinguished fires
And restored the dead to life;
He showed the Kara-Kyrgyz people
That he was their mighty camel.
He was a stronghold like a mottled mountain range,
A lion surpassing all the world.
When the noble lord was our shield,
The Kyrgyz of the Ala-Too
Said, ‘Where could suffering be?’
Will he begin a journey far away?
Will our dear lion-like hero
Mount and depart upon a journey,
Leaving his village desolate?
Before one can blink or raise a brow,
Before one can utter a word,
Will God not strike this nation?
Bereft of our precious lion,
Will He not leave these sobbing people
Like a fire extinguished?
The khagan’s nation is a teeming multitude,
As numerous as a mass of black worms.
If they destroy us, will God strike them down,
Or will they unleash a mighty war?
Bereft of our powerful lion,
Will they surround and slaughter us?
Is this how God will strike us?
We have no forest to flee into,
No Nogai to be our shelter,
No mountain refuge where we may hide,
And no renowned gray-maned lion
To deliver us
From toil, anguish, and affliction.
So wretched is this filthy world!
Bereft of our noble lion,
Dressed in black and swallowing blood,
We have been left in a night
So dark it blinds the eyes.
We have been left in a desert
Where no person can walk with sense
And no human being can endure.
We have been left in a grave
With neither door nor place of honor.
Oh, ill-fated people,
We have been left in a lake
Whose bottom is too deep to fathom.
Though the people gather in clans and encamp,
Bereft of the noble lion,
How shall the villages pitch camp?
What remedy can there be?
Many merely squint their eyes at us;
Many enemies jeer and mock us.
Many among us would unleash chaos,
Saying, ‘Father, a son of the Kyrgyz!’
And many nations bear us grudges.”
The people wailed and the nation clamored,
The multitudes grieving;
All the people sobbed,
Lamenting in anguish,
The nation wailing in sorrow.
It became clear that the dear, doomed gray wolf
Was truly departing,
And the people despaired of life.
They inhabited the Ala-Too;
No man could defeat them in combat,
And no enemy dared approach.
Their countless herds of four kinds
Spread in abundance across the land.
At the sight of their livestock and people,
The enemy’s courage failed.
Whenever a man came against them,
No attacking enemy could prevail.
Oh, blessed and beloved people,
They encamped in rows upon the ridges.
The people settled upon the summer pastures,
And their elders feasted on fat tails.
If an envious enemy came,
They chased him away like tumbleweed.
They climbed the ridges and summered there,
Tethering their prancing steeds.
When their many enemies confronted them,
Woe seethed for any who met them.
As long as our falcons lived,
When an enemy came against us,
In the days when joy endured,
We spilled his blood like water.
At Kara-Buura and Batkal,
When the countless Kyrgyz dwelt there,
Eating horse haunch when hungry,
When the Kyrgyz lived in high spirits,
When did the Kyrgyz ever grieve
Or consume themselves with fruitless sorrow?
If a foe came forth to fight,
If some deep and dire ordeal arose,
If there was a trench already dug,
If there was a challenger bent on enmity,
We said we would don
Impenetrable coats of mail.
Against the Chinese on our frontier,
Against Kangai on our flank,
Against the Kara-Chinese and Torgouts,
The Solon, Shibe, and Manchu,
Our champion used to say, ‘When my thoroughbred knots its tail,
My hour has come.’
When enraged at the kalda,
He said, ‘The time for my plea has come.’
While our valiant lions lived,
We crushed whomever we encountered
And defeated all who faced us.
While the dark lions bore
Their black-shafted Zulfiqar spears,
We said we would drive the foe away.
While the doomed heroes’ eyes were open,
We carved and ate the horse’s haunch.
We went about saying
We would make the whole wide world submit.
For the countless Kyrgyz people,
Where is another night like the holy Night of Power?
By day there was laughter, by night there were games;
Where now shall we find
A bright and radiant day?”—
So lamented the countless people;
The multitude wept and the nation cried out.
All the teeming people wept,
The white-bearded elders wept,
The children at play wept,
Every soul in the mighty mountains wept,
The trees on both banks wept,
And every living soul sobbed.
Their hearts were broken by grief;
The multitude, all the many young,
Could not laugh, their hearts distraught.
The vanity of this deceitful world
Was plainly revealed;
Great and small, old and young,
Not one was spared from heartbreak.
“Our dear lion will leave us,” they said,
And tears streamed from their eyes;
All the nation cried aloud,
And all the people raised a clamor.
For these people, Bakai and Kanykei
Were a mighty fortress,
A vast and surging mountain ridge.
Semetey and Külchoro
Were Mount Kap-Too, untouched by storms or wind,
Yielding no livestock to a claimant,
And no life to a demon—
A mountain that could never be broken.
They were the teeming Kyrgyz people’s defense,
A vast black fortress.
While the fierce gray wolf lived,
Though suffering descended upon the world,
We said, ‘Where could calamity be?’
While our warrior sultan lived,
When bored, we hunted deer;
When not, we poor souls
Played ordo for stakes amid loud rejoicing,
Played orompoy amid merry clamor,
Making them say, ‘Ah, the valiant Kyrgyz!’
We raised an uproar against every foe,
Serving as a stronghold that spared no life.
To those who knew and those who saw,
To those who heard and understood,
To any who merely narrowed their eyes at us,
And to the enemy who overran us,
We brought sheer affliction.
We were a broad, mottled mountain range
No living creature could cross.
We were the heroic Kyrgyz people,
Yielding to no one in all the world.
The sultan and stronghold have left the Kyrgyz,
The hero has left the people of the age,
The lion blessed by Khidr has departed.
Our glasslike eyes stare wildly;
Parted from our precious lion,
The nation wails in grief.
Bereft of our dear hero,
With no tail left to swish,
We stand like wild asses.
With no feet to stride forward,
We stand like snakes.
Will we become mounts
That do not even flick their ears as they walk?
When the enemy surrounds us,
Unable to charge and summon courage,
Will we become as the dead?
Will we cease to encamp
At Kan-Jailak, where the people spread?
Heeding no one’s word,
Unable to bear one another,
Will we cease to be a people?
Will this immense, incurable affliction
Leave us in turmoil?
Will painful misery and great conflict
Leave us in a single storm of chaos?
Bereft of our warrior lion,
We have fallen into disaster.
Our eyes dim and wander—
We have become blind.”—
So the nation clamored,
Yellowing like straw,
Amazed at the utter vanity
Of this battered world.
Every living creature
The Creator brought forth and set in motion;
All who knew, saw, or perceived,
The supreme decree of the Creator
Directed toward a single pit.
By His decree He fashioned
The eighteen thousand worlds.
Every living creature
Must cross this ominous black earth.
Oh Ala-Too, whose foothills are gold,
If only the Kyrgyz could dwell there forever!
If only our doomed prince Semetey,
His true kinsman Külchoro,
Poor Bakai and Kanykei,
And the noble lord’s wife Aichürök—
Alas, deceitful world!—
If only these, who should never die,
Had spines of iron!”
The whole nation cried out and wept,
Tormenting their fragile lives,
Unable to endure, lamenting,
Astonished that this exalted, painful world
Was empty at its core,
And marveling at it.
The great lion stood unmoving—
“Father, we have parted forever, dear lion!”—
The doomed hero stood unmoving.
